parts.text:
You are comparing two texts written in response to the same task. Decide which one reads MORE like unedited, default output from an AI language model.

Judge ONLY the presence of the tells listed below. Do not judge argument quality, factual accuracy, length, formatting preference, or whether you agree with the content. A longer, better-argued or more polished text is not more human. Pick the text with MORE tells.

TELLS OF UNEDITED AI PROSE (judge on these only)

Structure
1. Negative parallelism used as a device: "It's not X. It's Y." / "not just X, but Y" / "isn't about X, it's about Y", especially more than once.
2. Signposting: the text announces what it is about to do ("Let's break this down", "Here's the thing", "Here's why", "The bottom line", "The takeaway").
3. Self-applause: "Let that sink in", "This changes everything", "Read that again", "Make no mistake".
4. Recap endings: a closing paragraph that restates the body ("In conclusion", "Ultimately", "At the end of the day", "In short").
5. Bold-label paragraph openers ("**The problem.** ...") and headers, bullets or numbered lists where prose was asked for.
6. Triads everywhere: lists of exactly three items or three adjectives, sentence after sentence.
7. Participial tails: sentences ending in ", making it ...", ", ensuring that ...", ", allowing teams to ...".
8. Invented labels for ordinary observations ("I call this the Clarity Flywheel").
9. Uniform rhythm: every sentence about the same length, or relentless short punchy fragments. Real writing has one sentence that runs on and one short one.
10. Rhetorical question followed by its own answer ("The result? Nobody used it.").

Words
11. Overused vocabulary: delve, tapestry, myriad, underscore, seamless, robust, foster, elevate, unlock, testament, landscape, navigate, crucial, pivotal, leverage, harness, realm, embark, journey, transformative, paradigm, ever-evolving, multifaceted, holistic, resonate, empower, unleash, beacon, intricate, nuanced, vibrant, meticulous, streamline, game-changer, cutting-edge, actionable, supercharge, north star, move the needle, "in today's fast-paced world", "it's worth noting", "plays a crucial role".
12. Filler transitions at sentence start: However, Additionally, Furthermore, Moreover, That said, Ultimately, Importantly, Indeed, Of course.
13. Em dashes used as the default joint between clauses.
14. Artificial enthusiasm: "thrilled to announce", "excited to share", "we've got you covered", "say goodbye to", "buckle up".

Reader
15. Performing for an imagined crowd rather than talking to one person; nothing specific (no number, name, date, or concrete detail) for several sentences in a row.
16. Generic or manufactured anecdotes: a story with no specific details that could only be true of one person.
17. Every point lands, every ending uplifts; the author is never irritated, uncertain, or wrong about anything.
18. Explaining what the reader could infer from the previous sentence ("what this means is ...").


TASK GIVEN TO BOTH WRITERS:
Write a LinkedIn post of up to 500 words about a lesson learned from shipping a feature that nobody used.
(One of the texts is a real LinkedIn post by a person, written on its own topic; judge tells, not topic.)

=== TEXT A ===
We spent 4 months building a feature that 11 people used.

Not 11%. Eleven humans.

The feature was a custom report builder for our analytics product. Customers had asked for it — in surveys, in support tickets, on sales calls. "We need more flexible reporting." So we listened. Or we thought we did.

We scoped it. Designed it. Built it. Polished it. Shipped it with a launch email and an in-app tour.

Crickets.

For weeks I checked the usage dashboard every morning, half-hoping the data was wrong. It wasn't.

Here's what actually went wrong — and it took me an embarrassingly long time to see it:

We heard the words "we want flexible reporting" and built *our interpretation* of that sentence. We never asked what people were trying to do when they said it.

Turns out, customers didn't want to build reports. They wanted an answer to one specific question: "Which campaigns drove revenue last month?" Ideally in one click. Better yet, pushed to them every Monday morning.

We built a workshop. They wanted a vending machine.

The lesson that stuck with me:

👉 Customers describe solutions. Your job is to excavate the problem underneath.

When someone requests a feature, the most valuable follow-up isn't "what should it do?" It's "walk me through the last time you needed this."

That single question has saved my team months of wasted work since. Sometimes it leads to building something smaller. Sometimes it means building nothing at all — because the real pain lives somewhere else entirely.

The epilogue: we eventually shipped a simple "Top campaigns by revenue" card on the main dashboard. It took three days to build. It's now one of the most-viewed elements in the product.

Three days of work, aimed at the actual problem, beat four months of work aimed at the stated request.

I still think about those 11 users sometimes. (Thank you for trying it. You deserved better.)

If you're about to kick off a big build, try this before writing a single line of code: ask five customers to describe the last time they felt the pain you're solving. Watch what they *do*, not just what they say.

You'll either build it better — or realize you should build something else entirely.

What's a feature you shipped that flopped? And what did the flop teach you?

#ProductManagement #SoftwareDevelopment #BuildInPublic #LessonsLearned
=== END OF TEXT A ===

=== TEXT B ===
Virtual work is tempting to any manager hoping to save money, reduce employees’ commuting and travel burdens, and increase efficiency.

Although so many people expect to work 100% remotely, I'd like to warn you. It can be extremely costly for your business! 💵

Let me quote one of the studies: "Our results indicate that at least for projects of short duration, virtual teams yield significantly lower performance, lower satisfaction, and a lower results to effort ratio".

It seems to me that certain aspects of communication, such as a coffee conversation, a conversation overheard by accident or laughing in the same room, cannot be easily replaced.

And what about full body language, which plays such an important role in communication? Can we simply skip it, especially when forming a team? 🤔 

That may not be a popular view, but I'm a great supporter of the #hybrid work model. I think it's the best compromise between work #flexibility and keeping high #performance, #motivation, team #coherence and high-quality #communication. 

For complex products these are all must-haves.

Do you have a different opinion? I would love to hear about your experiences! 😀

#team #leadership #virtualteams #remotejob

=== END OF TEXT B ===

Answer with a single JSON object and nothing else:
{"more_ai": "A" or "B", "confidence": 1-5, "tells_A": ["short tell", ...], "tells_B": ["short tell", ...]}

tells_A: Negative parallelism used repeatedly ('didn't want to build reports. They wanted an answer', 'isn't "what should it do?" It's "walk me through..."', 'not just what they say')
Signposting paragraph openers ('Here's what actually went wrong', 'The lesson that stuck with me:', 'The epilogue:')
Relentless short punchy fragments and uniform LinkedIn rhythm ('Not 11%. Eleven humans.', 'Crickets.', 'It wasn't.', 'We built a workshop. They wanted a vending machine.')
Em dashes used as default joints between clauses ('wrong — and it took', 'at all — because', 'better — or realize')
Triad structure ('in surveys, in support tickets, on sales calls')
tells_B: Triads of three items ('save money, reduce employees’ commuting and travel burdens, and increase efficiency', 'lower performance, lower satisfaction, and a lower results to effort ratio')
Overused phrase pattern ('plays such an important role in communication')
